title: Why Can a JPEG Copy Be Larger Than the HEIC Original?
description: A JPEG compatibility copy can be larger than its HEIC original. Learn why conversion can increase storage and what to check before exporting more photos.
direct: A JPEG copy can be larger than the HEIC original. Choose JPEG for compatibility when it is required, then check the copy’s size separately.

cards.choice.heading: Start with the decision
cards.choice.body: Apple describes HEIF as offering more efficient compression than JPEG. A file extension does not determine a fixed size ratio. Pixel dimensions, image content and export choices also matter, so compare the actual files rather than expecting every conversion to shrink.
sections.detail-0.heading: Same picture, different encoding
sections.detail-0.body: A larger JPEG is not proof of added detail or a better original. It can simply use more bytes to represent the decoded picture. Conversely, a smaller file may discard detail. Do not repeatedly convert between lossy formats to chase a size number; return to the best original when preparing another copy.
sections.detail-1.heading: Know the conversion scope
sections.detail-1.body: It supports HEIC-to-JPEG and batch processing while leaving original photos untouched. The first three successful photo conversions are free, and each photo in a batch uses one conversion. HDR appearance and compatibility are separate checks. The illustration shows one scene with two format labels, not a fabricated quality comparison.
faqs.reader-question-1.heading: Why did the same pixel dimensions produce a larger JPEG?
faqs.reader-question-1.body: Different encoders, format settings and image content affect the byte count. Matching the width and height does not make file sizes equal.
faqs.reader-question-2.heading: Should I convert every HEIC before sharing?
faqs.reader-question-2.body: Convert the photos the recipient cannot open or specifically needs as JPEG. Test one copy first, then keep the original HEIC files.

steps.step-1.text: Keep the HEIC original and confirm whether the recipient really needs JPEG. A destination that accepts HEIC may not require conversion.
steps.step-2.text: Use PhotoFix’s HEIC-to-JPEG conversion to make a separate compatibility copy. Review the available export choices without assuming a particular compression-quality slider.
steps.step-3.text: Open the saved JPEG, inspect fine detail and check its file size in Files or the destination. Test that exact file before converting a large batch.
